# Text Data
## Recommended Reading

-   [*Text Mining with R*](https://www.tidytextmining.com/)
-   [`stringr` cheat sheet](https://evoldyn.gitlab.io/evomics-2018/ref-sheets/R_strings.pdf)

Text data is one of the most common type of data in the modern world. Usually, it is much more complicated than the numerical data thus we need to pre-process the data before we use it.

-   Humans generally suck at spelling and typing, so text data is messy

## Taylor Swift Tweets data

[A data set that captures tweets from Taylor Swift between 2009 and 2022.](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/thedevastator/taylor-swift-s-social-media-performance-tweet-en) We will briefly cover web scraping at the end of this course.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
library(readr)
TaylorSwift13 <- read_csv("TaylorSwift13.csv") 
glimpse(TaylorSwift13)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
library(readr)
TaylorSwift13 <- read_csv("../TaylorSwift13.csv") # Actual location is up one directory
glimpse(TaylorSwift13)
```

## Text Data Is Messy
Even though it is always exciting to work with the social media data, its messiness can make the analysis hard. 

It usually has a lot of missing data and text data is free of format.

Let's first focus on the tweet text itself and think about if we can create some variables that are easier to analyze from the text.

Before we extract the information, we need to convert all the text to lower cases (or upper if you preferred)

```{r}
TaylorSwift13$lowertext <- tolower(TaylorSwift13$content)
glimpse(TaylorSwift13$lowertext)
```

# Analyzing Text Data: Yes/no and counting questions

## Does "album" increase retweets?

Suppose, we want to know whether certain words in the text may increase the amount it is retweeted.

Recall the `str_detect` function in the previous labs. (The `stringr` package is a common package used for text data).

```{r}
TaylorSwift13 <- TaylorSwift13 %>%
  mutate(isAlbum = str_detect(lowertext, "album"))

table(TaylorSwift13$isAlbum) #39 exact matches
```


## `#`Hashtags
We can also look for a specific punctuation.

```{r}
TaylorSwift13 <- TaylorSwift13 %>%
  mutate(isHash = str_detect(lowertext, "#"))

table(TaylorSwift13$isHash) #111 tweets had a hashtag
```

We can even count how many hashtag in each text.

```{r}
TaylorSwift13 <- TaylorSwift13 %>%
  mutate(numHash = str_count(lowertext, "#"))

table(TaylorSwift13$numHash)
```

## Tweet length
There are some other basic information you can extract, like the length of the text

```{r}
TaylorSwift13 <- TaylorSwift13 %>%
  mutate(length = str_length(lowertext))

summary(TaylorSwift13$length) #summary of number of characters in each tweet
```

# Analyzing Text Data: getting into the text itself
## Parts of Speech

You can also do something fancy (but will take much longer time to run). For example, we can generate the part-of-speech tags for the words in the text and count how many nouns/verbs are in the text.

*Note:* It will be better to use the text without lower case transformation in the following detection.

-   Using universal parts of speech tag (https://universaldependencies.org/format.html)

```{r}
library(udpipe) #for parts of speech tagging

detect_ps = function(text){
  tokens = udpipe::udpipe(text, "english") #other langauages available
  NumNoun = tokens %>% filter(upos == "NOUN") %>% summarise(N = n()) %>% pull()
  NumVerb = tokens %>% filter(upos == "VERB") %>% summarise(N = n()) %>% pull()
  return(c(NumNoun, NumVerb))
}

detect_ps("	
surprise tonight at midnight i’ll be releasing my 8th studio album, folklore; an entire brand new album of songs i’ve poured all of my whims, dreams, fears, and musings into")
```
## Parts of Speech (2/3)
This can take a while to run. Here it is run on just the first 100 observations in the data
```{r}
#run function on column - can take a while to run
result = sapply(TaylorSwift13$content[1:100], detect_ps)

TaylorSwift13_sub = TaylorSwift13[1:100,] %>% 
  mutate(numNoun = result[1,], 
         numVerb = result[2,])

glimpse(TaylorSwift13_sub[,c(1,2,3,4,19,20,21)])
```

## Parts of Speech (3/3)
Other techniques like NER (Named entity recognition) can identify whether there is a Human name/Place in the text. See [the tutorial](https://rstudio-pubs-static.s3.amazonaws.com/230718_6d29404ebb2a444fa0d218917dd1ec67.html) if you are interested.

## Sentiment Analysis (1/2)

<!-- Words have meaning, thus an emotion can be associated with each word, and the text. Sentiment score is usually a number. If it is positive, it indicates the word/sentence has a positive meaning and vice versa. The scale for sentiment scores using the `syuzhet` method is a decimal and ranges from -1 (most negative) to +1 (most positive). If have a line of text, the function returns the sum of all the sentiment scores of meaningful words. -->
"Sentiment analysis" attempts to quantify the emotional valence of text

- Simple version: words are positive (like "happy" or "excited") or negative (like "fear" or "disappointed")
- Represent this with a positive or negative number

::: {.notes}
Articles, prepositions, etc. are neither positive nor negative. They're called 'stop words', we'll see them again near the end of the slides
:::

## Sentiment Analysis (2/2)
- `syuzhet` method identifies "meaningful" words and assigns each a sentiment score from $-1$ (totally negative) to $+1$ (totally positive)
- Sentences are scored by adding up values for each word

```{r}
library(syuzhet)

get_sentiment("happy")
get_sentiment("sad")
get_sentiment("It was a nice day even though we lost the game.")

TaylorSwift13$syuzhet <- get_sentiment(TaylorSwift13$lowertext)
summary(TaylorSwift13$syuzhet)

```

# Advanced Text Techniques

## IMDB Data {visibility="uncounted"}
In case you skipped over the "Try it yourself" section, you'll need to load the `imdb` data:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
imdb = read.csv("imdb.csv")
glimpse(imdb)
```

## Clean the categorical levels: Regular Expressions

::: {.callout-warning}
*Some people, when confronted with a problem, think "I know, I'll use regular expressions." Now they have two problems. - Jamie Zawinski*
:::

Sometimes we need to clean the data to generate a data that easier for analysis. We can find patterns in the data using [regular expressions](https://www.datacamp.com/tutorial/regex-r-regular-expressions-guide)

## Regular Expressions (2/3)
A **regular expression** is a sequence of characters that specify a match pattern to search for in a larger text


```{r}
num_string <- "phone: 123-456-7890, netid: 12345678, ssn: 123-45-6789" #<1>

phone <- str_extract(num_string,
                     "[0-9][0-9][0-9]-[0-9][0-9][0-9]-[0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9]") #<2>
phone

phone2 <- str_extract(num_string,
                      "[0-9]{3}-[0-9]{3}-[0-9]{4}") #{} - number of times look for pattern in a row #<3>
phone2
```
1. A string containing text, a phone number, and other numbers
2. A regular expression listing each digit individually
3. The `[0-9]{3}` means "a digit from 0 to 9, three times in a row.

## Regular Expression (3/3)
Suppose now we only take everyone's first profession.

```{r}
imdb$firstPro = gsub( #<1>
  ",.*",  # This is a regular expression to search for  #<2>
  "",     # This is the new text to replace it with #<3>
  imdb$primaryProfession) #<4>
#extract everything to first comma. Replace everything after first column with a blank

head(imdb[,c(2,5,10)])
table(imdb$firstPro)
```
1. "sub" is short for "substitution"
2. Find the part of the string that looks like a comma followed by any number of characters
3. Replace that piece with nothing
4. Apply this to the `primaryProfession` column

## Regular Expressions: Pop Quiz

Which of the following regular expressions would match a *valid* variable names in `R` and *not* match any *invalid* variable names?

A. `[0-9]+[a-z]*`
B. `[a-zA-Z]+[a-zA-Z0-9_]*`
C. `valid_variable_name`

::: {.notes}
This is intentionally tricky. A is wrong because variable names cannot start with a number. B is correct, since a variable name can start with a letter, and then have a mix of letters, numbers, and underscores. C would match the name "valid variable name", which is a valid variable name! It would also not match anything else. Therefore, as worded, the answer to the question is B and C.

This is definitely way more tricky than we need to get for this class, but it *is* important to think about the logic behind regular expressions and how they're used. Recall the quote from the first slide about REs.
:::

## Find and Replace

With regular expressions:
```{r}
fruits <- c("one apple", "two pears", "three bananas")

str_replace_all(fruits,
                "[aeiou]",  # Regular expression
                "-")        # What to replace it with
```

With a mapping:
```{r}
str_replace_all(fruits,
                c("one" = "1",     #<1>
                  "two" = "2",     #<1>
                  "three" = "3"))  #<1>
```
1. These lines create a mapping, also known as an associative array or dictionary

## Separating/Extracting Information from Columns

Going back to our Taylor Swift example.


```{r}
TaylorSwift13$year <- str_sub(TaylorSwift13$date, 1 , 4)
glimpse(TaylorSwift13$year)

```

One more note: the date/time data can also be treated as the text data. You can choose to extract only the year/month from the complete timestamps.
```{r}
ts <- separate_wider_delim(TaylorSwift13, date, delim = " ", 
                     names = c("date_new", "time"))
```

## Side note: Dates and Times {visibility="uncounted"}

Dates and times can get messy (what time zone? Is it Daylight Savings Time? Is it 12-hour or 24-hour? Etc.)

Luckily, the `lubridate` package can handle a lot of that messiness for you, allowing you to deal with dates and times "abstractly"
```{r}
glimpse(TaylorSwift13$date) # notice the type is POSIXct

library(lubridate)
months(TaylorSwift13$date)
```

## Summarizing the text

Instead of generating new variables to fit a model, sometimes we just what to know what those texts are about.

- One way to do this is to generate a word cloud, which displays the most frequent words.

It is difficult to analyze a *sentence* of text.
- We can't filter out words or count which occur most frequently since it is made up of multiple words, and the order matters
- Hence, we need to covert it into *tokens*. - A *token* is a meaningful unit of text that can be used for further analysis.
  + (Yes, these are the same tokens being referred to in LLM usage)

## Tokenizing Text
We create tokens using the `unnest_tokens` function.

```{r}
tweet_words <- TaylorSwift13 %>%
  dplyr::select(content) %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, content)

head(tweet_words) #puts each word on own row
```

```{r}
top10 <- tweet_words %>% count(word,sort=T) %>% slice(1:10) 

ggplot(top10, aes(x = reorder(word, n, function(n) -n), y = n)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") + 
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 60, hjust = 1))
```

## Stop words
Stop words are words that do not have meaning in the text, like "the" and "a".

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
glimpse(stop_words)
```
```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
my_stop_words <- stop_words %>% dplyr::select(word) %>% 
  bind_rows(data.frame(word = c("https", "t.co", "rt", "amp")))

tweet_words_interesting <- tweet_words %>% anti_join(my_stop_words) 
#removed Stop words
```
```{r, fig.height=6}
#| output-location: "slide"
top10 <- tweet_words_interesting %>% count(word,sort=T) %>% slice(1:10) 

ggplot(top10, aes(x = reorder(word, n, function(n) -n), y = n)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") + 
  presentation_theme + 
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 60, hjust = 1))
```

## Generating a Word Cloud
You can create a Word Cloud (only if output is `html`!) - https://r-graph-gallery.com/196-the-wordcloud2-library.html

```{r}
#| output-location: "slide"
library(wordcloud2)

t <- tweet_words_interesting %>%
  group_by(word) %>%
  tally(sort = TRUE) %>%
  filter(n > 5)

wordcloud2(t)

```

## Sentiment Analysis Again

You can also show the general trend of sentiments in all the words.
```{r, warning=FALSE, eval=FALSE}
#| code-line-numbers: "2,3|4,5|8,9|10"
#library(textdata)
nrc_lex <- get_sentiments("nrc") #<1>
fn_sentiment <- tweet_words_interesting %>% left_join(nrc_lex) #<1>
fn_sentiment %>% filter(!is.na(sentiment)) %>% #<2>
  group_by(sentiment) %>% #<2>
  summarise(n=n()) #<3>

bing_lex <- get_sentiments("bing") #<4>
fn_sentiment <- tweet_words_interesting %>% left_join(bing_lex) #<5>
fn_sentiment %>% filter(!is.na(sentiment)) %>% group_by(sentiment) %>% summarise(n=n()) #<6>
```
